title: What is the difference between physical/streaming replication (byte-level WAL shipping, exact binary copy, same DB engine only) and logical replication (row-level change events, can replicate selectively, cross-version/cross-engine possible)?

s1_definition.profdef: Physical (streaming) replication ships the write-ahead log at the byte level, so the replica is an exact binary copy of the primary's data files — it requires the same engine and major version and replicates everything. Logical replication decodes the WAL into row-level change events (insert/update/delete per table) and applies them, which lets you replicate selected tables, transform data, and even cross versions or engines.
s1_definition.analogy: Physical replication is like photocopying every page of National Bank of India's ledger exactly, so the copy is byte-for-byte identical — but both books must be the same edition. Logical replication is like reading out each change ("credit 50000 to SAV2001") and writing it into another book that could be a different edition or layout, and you can choose to copy only the accounts ledger, not the whole library.
s1_definition.oneliner: Physical = exact binary copy of the whole cluster, same engine; logical = selective row-level change events, cross-version/engine capable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Physical (streaming) replication ships the write-ahead log at the byte level, so the replica is an exact binary copy of the primary's data files — it requires the same engine and major version and replicates everything. Logical replication decodes the WAL into row-level change events (insert/update/delete per table) and applies them, which lets you replicate selected tables, transform data, and even cross versions or engines.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Physical replication is like photocopying every page of National Bank of India's ledger exactly, so the copy is byte-for-byte identical — but both books must be the same edition. Logical replication is like reading out each change ("credit 50000 to SAV2001") and writing it into another book that could be a different edition or layout, and you can choose to copy only the accounts ledger, not the whole library.

**One line to remember:** Physical = exact binary copy of the whole cluster, same engine; logical = selective row-level change events, cross-version/engine capable.

sections.s2_technical:
Physical/streaming replication continuously sends WAL bytes to a standby that replays them, producing an identical copy of every database, table, and index. It is efficient and the standard way to run a hot standby and read replicas, but the replica is read-only, must match the primary's major version and architecture, and cannot replicate a subset.

Logical replication uses logical decoding to turn WAL into a stream of row changes published per table; a subscriber applies them. This enables selective replication (only certain tables), consolidating many sources into one, zero-downtime major-version upgrades (replicate old to new, then switch), and cross-engine pipelines via change-data-capture tools like Debezium. The trade-offs: it does not replicate DDL automatically, large transactions and initial snapshots cost more, and sequences and some object types need care.

Senior nuance: use physical replication for high-availability standbys and read scaling where you want an exact clone, and logical replication for selective feeds, upgrades, and streaming changes into Kafka/warehouses. They are often combined — physical for the DR standby, logical CDC for the analytics pipeline.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs an exact hot standby for failover and, separately, a feed of only the accounts and transactions tables into a Kafka-based analytics pipeline. This is exactly physical versus logical: physical for the full clone, logical for the selective change stream.

The demo has a `WalShipper` with `physicalReplicate()` (replays raw byte records for all tables) and `logicalReplicate()` (emits row-change events only for a chosen table), over Rajesh's data.

wal-replication-service/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/bank/wal/
    ├── WalDemo.java

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__logical_repl.sql (PostgreSQL)
-- Physical: configured at cluster level (recovery.conf / primary_conninfo) — replays ALL WAL.
-- Logical: publish only selected tables
CREATE TABLE accounts (id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(15,2));
CREATE TABLE audit_internal (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT);

-- Publish ONLY accounts (and transactions) to subscribers — selective
CREATE PUBLICATION analytics_pub FOR TABLE accounts;   -- audit_internal NOT replicated

-- On the subscriber (could be a newer major version or a CDC sink):
-- CREATE SUBSCRIPTION analytics_sub
--   CONNECTION 'host=primary dbname=bankdb'
--   PUBLICATION analytics_pub;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
replication:
  physical:
    standby: dr-delhi        # exact binary clone, same version
  logical:
    publication: analytics_pub
    tables: [accounts, transactions]
    sink: kafka://trade.cdc
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three raw WAL records spanning accounts and an internal audit table, plus three decoded row events.

Step 1: physicalReplicate copies all three raw records verbatim to the standby — accounts and audit_internal alike — producing an exact clone.

Step 2: logicalReplicate decodes the row events and keeps only those for the published accounts table, dropping the audit_internal insert.

Step 3: Two accounts events flow to the Kafka analytics sink; the internal table never leaves, showing selective replication.

```text
2026-10-25 18:30:00 [INFO] PHYSICAL replicated 3 WAL records (all tables, exact copy)
2026-10-25 18:30:00 [INFO] LOGICAL published 2 row events for [accounts]
to-kafka -> UPDATE accounts {id:SAV2001,balance:950000}
to-kafka -> INSERT accounts {id:CUR3001,balance:250000}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Primary WAL
    │
    ├─ PHYSICAL (byte-level)                 ├─ LOGICAL (row-level decode)
    │  replay ALL tables verbatim            │  filter to PUBLICATION tables
    │  → exact binary standby                │  → accounts events only
    │  same engine + major version           │  cross-version / cross-engine ok
    ▼                                        ▼
  DR hot standby (read-only clone)          Kafka CDC → analytics warehouse
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — WalShipper ═══

  ┌─ Choice: physical (full clone) vs logical (selective CDC) ─┐
  │  SOLID S: shipper only moves/decodes WAL                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          WalShipper          │
  │  + physicalReplicate(bytes)  │  all tables, exact copy
  │  + logicalReplicate(evts,pub)│  filter to published tables
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Note: logical does NOT replicate DDL automatically; sequences need care.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Physical, or streaming, replication ships the write-ahead log at the byte level, so the standby replays those bytes and becomes an exact binary copy of the entire cluster. It is efficient and is the standard way to run a hot standby and read replicas, but the replica is read-only, must match the primary's major version and architecture, and copies everything with no way to select a subset. Logical replication instead decodes the write-ahead log into row-level change events published per table, which a subscriber applies, enabling selective replication, zero-downtime major-version upgrades, and cross-engine streaming through change-data-capture tools.

In our National Bank of India platform I use both. Physical streaming replication maintains an exact hot standby in the disaster-recovery site for fast failover, and logical replication publishes only the accounts and transactions tables into a Kafka change-data-capture pipeline that feeds the analytics warehouse, deliberately leaving internal audit tables behind. The trade-offs I keep in mind are that logical replication does not carry DDL automatically, needs care with sequences and initial snapshots, and costs more on very large transactions, whereas physical replication is cheaper and exact but locks me to the same engine and version. The line I remember is: physical is an exact binary copy of the whole cluster on the same engine, while logical is selective row-level change events that can cross versions and engines.
